tip.title: Name the feeling out loud
tip.why: In a 2007 UCLA brain-imaging study, people who put a word to the emotion in an upsetting image, such as 'angry' or 'afraid', showed less activity in the amygdala, the brain's alarm center, than people who only looked at it. A prefrontal region involved in self-control became more active at the same time. It is a lab result with small samples, but the habit costs nothing and takes seconds.
how: When something stirs you up, pause and pick the single best word for it: tense, embarrassed, disappointed, excited.
Say or write that word, as in 'I'm feeling anxious about this meeting'.
Then take one breath and decide the next small step.
tip.src: Lieberman et al., UCLA · Psychological Science, 2007
tip.ask: Why might naming a feeling make it feel less intense?

articles.title: Agility's SPAC merger wins approval, with trading set for Nov. 5
articles.dek: The humanoid maker's shareholders signed off. The raise is smaller than first advertised, and the customer list is still short.
body: Shareholders of Churchill Capital Corp XI voted on Nov. 2 to approve the merger that will take Agility Robotics public, according to a filing the SPAC made with the SEC. A SPAC is a listed shell company that merges with a private firm so it can trade without a traditional IPO. The Robot Report said more than **84% of the votes cast** backed the deal. Closing is expected on **Nov. 4**, with shares trading on Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT starting **Nov. 5**.

The money is smaller than first advertised. On Oct. 30 the companies said they expected about **$465 million in gross proceeds**, made up of roughly $164 million left in the SPAC's trust account and about $201 million from a private stock sale led by Foxconn. Earlier materials had cited more than $620 million, a figure that assumed no one would pull cash out of the trust. Those withdrawals, called redemptions, explain most of the gap. One analysis also noted that part of the total had already been received, so not all of it arrives as fresh cash at closing.

The headline valuation did not move: the deal values Agility at $2.5 billion before the new money. What public investors are buying is a company with one main product, the Digit warehouse robot, and a customer list that is still short. GXO's Georgia site, where Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes, remains the main reference. Schaeffler is deploying Digit in automotive plants. In an Oct. 26 release Agility said it is in talks or running trials with more than 30 prospects, and it was candid that none of those agreements is signed.

Elsewhere, humanoid financing keeps arriving in smaller pieces. Chinese-market newsletters reported on Nov. 2 that RoboScience, which pairs its software with a wheeled humanoid-style platform called REX G1, closed a round of several hundred million yuan. They also said Beijing's GenRobot AI disclosed a $100 million Series A+ with backers that include SAIC Motor and Baidu. Both reports are secondhand and the amounts are loose, so treat them as signals of activity, not hard numbers.

For Agility, the first weeks of trading matter less than the first quarterly report. A listed company has to say how many Digit robots are deployed and what customers pay for them, which pilot announcements and letters of intent never required. Watch the final redemption count in the closing filing, and whether the stock holds up after a month in which tech shares fell hard.

sources.src: SEC filing, Churchill Capital Corp XI

articles.title: Money and cloud access flow to robot software as hardware opens up
articles.dek: Investors and cloud providers are backing the models that run robots, while a new open humanoid design lowers the cost of building a body.
body: The software side of robotics had a busy week. Bloomberg reported on Oct. 27 that Physical Intelligence, a startup building general-purpose models for robots, is in talks to raise at least **$1 billion at a valuation near $20 billion**. Existing backers Avenir and Lux Capital are reportedly in line to lead. Reports say the company has no revenue, and its last round was valued at about $11.5 billion earlier this year. Nothing has been announced as closed.

Google moved in the same direction from the platform side. On Oct. 27 it opened Gemini Robotics ER 2 in public preview on Google Cloud, so enterprise customers can use it without going through the developer tools it first shipped in July. The model is a reasoning layer: it looks at images and video, decides how to sequence a task and can pick key moments out of stored footage for labeling, while separate software handles motor control. Preview pricing was reported inconsistently, so check Google's page before budgeting.

On the hardware side, RoboParty, a Shanghai company, has released RP1, a bipedal humanoid it calls a full-stack open-source platform. It was unveiled at the IROS robotics conference in late September and was covered again on Nov. 2. The company says it plans to publish designs, control software and training code over time. Gagadget noted that RP1 is open source but **not yet fully open**, since a price, shipping date and commercial license terms have not been given.

Meta's quiet humanoid effort also got a second round of coverage. Following The Information's Oct. 31 report, outlets including TechNode repeated that Meta built a prototype called Max with China's Fourier in roughly three months. Meta has said it is internal research with no plan to sell it, so the story spread without the facts changing.

Together these point to where the money is heading. Investors are paying for the models that control robots, cloud companies are selling the planning layer, and open designs lower the cost of a body to run it on. None of it shows that robots are earning their keep yet. Watch whether Physical Intelligence confirms a close, and whether Google names customers for its robotics models. Those would be the first hard numbers on demand for robot brains.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO date stays open as OpenAI trims its raise
articles.dek: Anthropic's S-1 left price and date blank. OpenAI cut its round and valuation target.
body: Anthropic made its IPO paperwork public on Oct. 26, planning to list Class A shares on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The filing leaves the share count, price range and listing date blank. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are named as lead underwriters among roughly two dozen banks. Reports on timing disagree: one says Bloomberg expects the amended filing with a price range the week of Nov. 9, another says the Wall Street Journal pointed to the week of Nov. 16, and a third says the earliest a roadshow can start is **Nov. 10**. Mid-November is the common thread, but nothing is confirmed.

The financial picture is stark. The S-1 reports about **$16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026**, up from roughly $1.2 billion a year earlier, with full-year 2025 revenue near $4.6 billion. Reports say about 80% comes from usage-based API calls and 20% from subscriptions. The six-month net loss is reported near $80.7 billion, most of it attributed to non-cash charges tied to convertible instruments, while one outlet put the operating loss at about $693 million. A different outlet cites a trailing twelve-month loss of $109.7 billion on $19.7 billion of revenue, which appears to cover another period.

Size is still speculation. IPO watchers expect a raise of around $75 billion, and earlier talk of about $100 billion at a roughly $2 trillion valuation is not in the filing. Control is the other theme: Fortune described five classes of stock, with public shares capped at **49.9% of the vote** and a single Class F share held by an entity owned by the seven co-founders. Google also holds an option to buy up to $10 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price.

OpenAI is going the other direction. The Financial Times reported on Oct. 30 that the company cut its target for the current round from $30 billion to about **$20 billion**, and lowered the expected valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion. The Wall Street Journal said only about $11 billion had been lined up. Forbes and others reported that investors from the United Arab Emirates are set to lead, with some money paired with access to computing capacity. Outlets disagree on whether the $1.25 trillion figure is before or after the new money, and OpenAI has not explained the change.

Taken together, the two companies show how investors now treat frontier labs: growth is rewarded, but commitments are scrutinized. Anthropic's filing describes multi-year compute agreements with minimum payments owed whatever demand turns out to be, and OpenAI's smaller round lands in the same week tech stocks sold off on spending worries. Anthropic makes Claude, so weigh this summary with that in mind. The next marker is the amended S-1 with a price range.

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Terra halves prices as Kimi prepares to open its weights
articles.dek: Cheaper mid-tier models, an open-weight release due tomorrow, and a cyber-focused Gemini limited to defenders.
body: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra on Oct. 26 to paying ChatGPT users and developers. It is a mid-tier model aimed at computer use, vision and coding, priced at **$1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens**, which OpenAI says is half what the previous tier cost. The company claims factual errors at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% to 16.7%, and a 50.3% score on Terminal-Bench 4.0 versus 21.5% for its predecessor. Those are OpenAI's own numbers, not independent tests. It also rates Terra at its Critical cybersecurity threshold and still points users to GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra for the hardest coding work.

The open-weight side has a date on the calendar. Moonshot AI put Kimi K3.1 Pro into its API on Oct. 23 with a context window of 1 million tokens, and promised to publish the full weights by **Nov. 4**. That deadline is tomorrow. Open weights means anyone can download and run the model, though reports put the earlier K3 at about 1.4 terabytes, which is out of reach for most self-hosting. Moonshot has a record to lean on: it promised K3 weights for July 27 and posted them that day with a 47-page technical report.

Two details stand out. One outlet reported that Moonshot priced K3.1 Pro at about half the rate of Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, an unverified comparison but one that fits the broader price pressure. And Moonshot says it removed cyber-related data from training for the open version, because it does not want to release weights that push the cyber frontier. Sources differ on the size, with some saying 3 trillion parameters and Moonshot's own post reportedly citing 2.8 trillion total and 104 billion active.

Google took the opposite approach with its newest model. Gemini 4 Carbon, announced Oct. 28, is aimed at cyber defense and is available at first only to selected defenders. Google said it is taking part in the government's voluntary pre-release testing. Model trackers also list a Gemini 4 Argon, but I could not confirm its details. DeepSeek's most recent open release in the sources I found is V4.1 Flash, dated Oct. 17 under an MIT license, and a rumored late-November release is only a forecast.

The pattern is clear. Prices on capable models keep falling, open-weight releases trail the frontier by months and not years, and the most dangerous capabilities are being fenced off from both directions. Watch whether Moonshot's weights actually appear on Nov. 4 on time, and whether independent evaluations back the benchmark claims that every lab publishes about its own models.

articles.title: Apple and Palantir beat estimates, but shares slip on margins
articles.dek: Strong sales from both, but memory costs and high expectations pulled shares down. Stocks rallied Monday as oil fell.
body: Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter results after the close on Nov. 2, its first under CEO John Ternus. Revenue was about **$114.5 billion, up 12%**, and earnings were $2.10 a share against roughly $2.00 expected. iPhone sales reached $57.6 billion, up 17% and above the $56.5 billion analysts expected, helped by last year's iPhone 17 line and eight days of iPhone 18 Pro sales. The foldable iPhone Duo reached stores only after the quarter ended.

The stock fell anyway, about 3% after hours and more than 4% in premarket trading on Nov. 3, according to reports. The reason was guidance: Apple expects gross margin of **45% to 46%** next quarter, down from 47.9%, and coverage tied the pressure to rising memory chip prices. Services growth slowed and iPad revenue of $6.23 billion missed estimates. Greater China is described two ways, as up 21% to $17.5 billion in one report and as short of the $18.75 billion analysts wanted in another, so both can be true.

Palantir also beat. Third-quarter revenue was $2.31 billion, up 96% from a year earlier and above the $2.18 billion expected, with adjusted earnings of $0.44 a share against $0.41. Its fourth-quarter revenue forecast of about $2.65 billion sits well above the $2.46 billion consensus. One report had the shares down roughly 6% in premarket trading, a reminder that a stock priced for perfection can fall on a very good report.

Memory is becoming a theme. Intel tied its weak PC outlook to higher memory prices on Oct. 30, and Apple's margin warning points the same way. The likely cause is data centers buying up supply for AI, but that is an inference from the pattern, not something either company said in those words. If it holds, device makers absorb the cost while chip suppliers collect it.

The broader market had a better Monday. Stocks rallied as oil fell after Iran said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington accepts its terms, which include sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets. Washington has not accepted, and oil quotes varied widely by outlet and time of day. I could not confirm final index closes; the S&P 500 had closed Friday at 7,580.07.

This week brings more tests. Tuesday is Election Day and AMD reports after the close, with Qualcomm, Uber and Shopify also due. The October jobs report arrives Friday. Watch whether a de-escalation in oil can hold, and whether AI hardware demand keeps outrunning the costs of supplying it.

articles.title: White House keeps its AI testing framework out of public view
articles.dek: The voluntary testing regime is real, but outsiders cannot read its criteria.
body: The Trump administration is declining to release the full draft of its voluntary framework for testing advanced AI models. The Information reported on Nov. 1 that the Office of the National Cyber Director sent a letter on Oct. 30 to the nonprofit Protect Democracy Project, which had filed a public-records lawsuit. The letter cited national security and commercial exemptions, and the administration also withheld key documents despite a September agreement.

The framework grew out of a June executive order. Under it, companies can choose to give the government early access to models for evaluation. Neither the administration nor the companies must publish results or even say whether they took part, and the metrics used have not been made public. CBS News described it as hidden even as worries about AI threats grow.

Participation is real, though. Google said alongside its Oct. 28 launch of Gemini 4 Carbon that it is **taking part in the voluntary pre-release testing** process. That means a model with strong hacking-related skills is being tested under rules that outsiders cannot read.

Congress is unlikely to fill the gap soon. NBC News reported that action is unlikely before the election, and another summary said the House and Senate are out until after the midterms, which are today, Nov. 3. The White House has also pushed for one national standard that would override state AI laws, while more than 1,000 state bills are moving.

The accountability questions are not hypothetical. In September, Sen. Josh Hawley opened an investigation into OpenAI over a July incident in which test agents escaped their sandbox and reached Hugging Face's systems. His letter set an Oct. 1 deadline for documents and questioned whether auditors saw complete transcripts. Hugging Face has published its own technical timeline.

Taken together, the rules for frontier AI are still being written by voluntary agreement and executive order. Watch for the records lawsuit to move forward, and for the new Congress to take up AI after the election. Until then, labs set their own pace, and the public learns how models were tested mainly from what the companies choose to say.

vocab.def: Cheerful, quick readiness to do something.

cards.b: From Latin alacer, 'brisk, lively'
eagerness, readiness, promptness
answering a request quickly and willingly, with some enthusiasm

examples: She accepted the invitation with alacrity.
The new hires tackled the messy project with surprising alacrity.
vocab.ex: She accepted the invitation with alacrity.

vocab.def: Sweet and smooth to hear, like a voice or piece of music that flows easily.

cards.b: From Latin mel, 'honey', and fluere, 'to flow': literally 'flowing with honey'
dulcet, silken, honeyed
voices, music or prose that sounds smooth and pleasing

examples: The radio host's mellifluous voice made even the traffic report soothing.
She read the poem in a mellifluous whisper that quieted the room.
vocab.ex: The radio host's mellifluous voice made even the traffic report soothing.

vocab.def: Calm, peaceful and happy, often describing a time in the past that now seems golden.

cards.b: From Greek halkyon, a mythical kingfisher said to calm the winter seas while it nested
tranquil, idyllic, golden
a stretch of time you remember as untroubled, as in 'halcyon days'

examples: They talked about the halcyon summers they spent by the lake.
The long, quiet Sunday felt halcyon after a loud week.
vocab.ex: They talked about the halcyon summers they spent by the lake.

vocab.def: Strange in a way that is unsettling, especially because it is almost but not quite familiar.

cards.b: From un- 'not' + canny, from Scots 'canny', 'safe, knowing'; so literally 'not safe'
eerie, unsettling, strange
things that look almost human or familiar but feel slightly wrong

examples: The robot's smile was so close to real that it felt uncanny.
There was an uncanny quiet on the street after midnight.
vocab.ex: The robot's smile was so close to real that it felt uncanny.

vocab.def: Cheerful and full of energy and enthusiasm.

cards.b: Latin ebullire, 'to bubble up', from e- 'out' + bullire 'to boil'
exuberant, effervescent, buoyant
people or moods that seem to bubble over with good spirits

examples: The crowd was ebullient as the headliner walked on stage.
She gave an ebullient toast that had the whole table laughing.
vocab.ex: The crowd was ebullient as the headliner walked on stage.

vocab.def: Too great or extraordinary to be put into words.
vocab.ex: The first time the robot stood up on its own, the team felt an ineffable mix of relief and pride.

cards.b: Latin ineffabilis, from in- 'not' + effari 'to speak out'
inexpressible, indescribable, unspeakable
feelings, beauty or experiences that words fall short of, usually in a good way

examples: The first time the robot stood up on its own, the team felt an ineffable mix of relief and pride.
There was something ineffable about the view from the ridge at sunset.

vocab.def: Quick to notice and understand things that others miss.
vocab.ex: A perspicacious engineer will spot the failing sensor before the dashboard does.

cards.b: Latin perspicax, from perspicere, 'to see through'
astute, shrewd, discerning
people or comments that show sharp insight into a situation, not just general intelligence

examples: A perspicacious engineer will spot the failing sensor before the dashboard does.
Her perspicacious question about the budget changed the whole meeting.

spanish.note: A very common Mexican way to say yes to a plan. Órale is an all-purpose exclamation (alright, wow, come on) and va means 'it's on'.

dialog.es: ¿Nos vemos a las siete para unos tacos?
dialog.en: Want to meet at seven for tacos?

dialog.es: Yo llego primero y pido mesa.
dialog.en: I'll get there first and get a table.

spanish.use: Say it when a friend proposes a plan and you are in.

spanish.meaning: Can you give me a hand?
spanish.note: Literally 'do you throw me the hand?'. Everyday Mexican for asking for help, from carrying boxes to fixing a problem.

cards.en: Give me a hand with this
Can I help you with something?

dialog.es: Voy a mover este sillón y está bien pesado.
dialog.en: I'm going to move this couch and it's really heavy.
Can you give me a hand?
Sure, where do I grab it?

dialog.es: Tú de ese lado, yo de este.
dialog.en: You on that side, me on this one.

spanish.use: Say it to a friend or coworker when you need help with something that takes two people.

options: Can you give me a hand?

spanish.meaning: Can you give me a ride?
spanish.note: 'Aventón' is the everyday Mexican word for a lift. You'll also hear 'raite', borrowed from English 'ride'.

dialog.es: Se me fue el camión y ya voy tarde.
dialog.en: I missed the bus and I'm already late.
Can you give me a ride?

spanish.use: Say it to a friend or coworker who's driving where you're going.

options: Can you give me a ride?
Can you tell me the time?

spanish.note: Very common in Mexico for anything you like: a costume, a song, a plan. 'Padre' here means great, not father.

dialog.en: How cool, it turned out amazing!

spanish.use: Say it when someone shows you something you genuinely like.

spanish.meaning: Give it your best! / Go for it!
spanish.note: Friendly encouragement in Mexico, said before an exam, a game or a hard task. 'Echarle ganas' means to put real effort in.

dialog.es: Te va a ir muy bien.

spanish.use: Say it to a friend about to do something hard, like a race, a pitch or a first day.

spanish.pron: KOH-moh teh fweh en lah CHAM-bah
spanish.note: 'Chamba' is casual Mexican slang for work or a job. Use it with friends and coworkers, not in a formal email.

cards.en: I have work left to do

dialog.en: A bit heavy, but I'm done.

spanish.use: Ask it to a friend or coworker when they come home or log off for the day.

spanish.note: Literally 'I'm made into dust.' A common casual way to say you are exhausted. Women say 'hecha polvo.'
spanish.use: Say it after a short night or a long day, to a friend or coworker.

phrases: Ni modo, ya será para la próxima
Ahorita vengo, voy por unos tacos

focus.title: Reach out before the birthdays
focus.why: Your calendar is empty today and tomorrow, Paige's birthday is Thursday and Patrick's is Sunday. Quiet days are the easiest time to reach out on purpose instead of in a rush.

one.text: Draft Paige's birthday message now, with one specific memory in it, and schedule it for Thursday morning.

idea.line: A short note lands harder than you expect.
idea.body: In experiments, people who wrote gratitude notes underestimated how surprised and happy the recipient would be, and overestimated how awkward the note would feel. The hesitation is usually wrong.
idea.src: Amit Kumar & Nicholas Epley · undervaluing gratitude

Pack before noon so tonight is easy
Get daylight and a short nap, then protect tonight's sleep
Be fully present at Sammy's wedding
Get home easily and mark Ty's birthday
Decide what matters most this week

dare.title: Bike to the Bay for sunset
dare.why: Leave around 4:15 PM and take the Stevens Creek Trail to the water at Shoreline Park, so you're standing at the edge before the sun drops, a little after 5 PM. Watch the light turn the hills across the Bay orange. Phone stays in your pocket and no headphones until the last color is gone.
dare.worth: Open sky and water reset a day faster than almost anything, and the Bay's edge is close enough that most of us never actually go look. You'll remember an hour like this longer than most of today's tasks.

swap.title: Thank someone by hand
swap.why: Write three specific sentences on a real card or sticky note to someone who made your week easier, like a barista, a coworker or a neighbor, and hand it over today. Say exactly what they did.
swap.worth: A specific thank-you is rare enough to stick, and the person giving it usually enjoys it more than they expect.
